analysis.one_liner: Restricts fees, penalties, and insurance add-ons in high-cost mortgages and makes lenders verify borrowers can repay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee from May 2002 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted 'predatory' high-cost home loans — loans carrying interest rates or fees far above what most borrowers pay. It would have banned balloon payments, capped prepayment penalties, barred lenders from financing expensive single-premium credit insurance into the loan, limited the points and fees lenders could roll into the balance, required lenders to actually check that a borrower could afford the payments, and stopped lenders from forcing borrowers into private arbitration instead of court. It also raised fines for violations and extended the time borrowers have to sue. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners, especially older and lower-income homeowners targeted with high-cost refinance loans, who would face fewer fee-stacking tricks, no balloon payments, a real ability-to-repay check, and stronger rights to cancel bad loans and sue in court.

how_it_helps.text: Lenders could not make a high-cost mortgage unless they verified, from income and obligations independent of the borrower's own statements, that the borrower could make the payments — the kind of check that was absent before the 2008 housing crash.
The bill banned all balloon payments, capped prepayment penalties to a narrow 24-month window, and barred creditors from financing prepayment fees on their own refinanced loans into the new balance.

It prohibited packing single-premium credit life, disability, or property insurance into the loan up front — a practice that could add thousands to the debt for coverage that lost value if the loan was paid off early.

It capped the points and fees a lender could finance at the greater of 3% of the loan or $600, counted all mortgage broker compensation toward that cap, and barred mandatory arbitration so borrowers could take disputes to court.

It strengthened remedies: civil penalties rose from $2,000 to $10,000 per violation, class-action caps were raised, the statute of limitations for these claims extended to three years, and waivers of the right to cancel became void if the lender encouraged them.

analysis.who_pays: Subprime and high-cost mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers whose compensation would count against the fee cap, and single-premium credit insurers, whose fee and insurance revenue on these loans would shrink; some of that cost could reach marginal borrowers as scarcer credit.

drawbacks.text: Tight rules on high-cost loans can shrink the supply of credit to borrowers with poor credit histories, who might face fewer loan options or higher prices on the loans that remain.
New counseling notices, disclosure statements, verification, and quarterly credit reporting duties add compliance costs that lenders could pass through in loan pricing.

The definitions (rates 6–8 points above Treasury yields, or points and fees above 5% of the loan) catch only the highest-cost slice of the market, so many expensive but sub-threshold loans would go unregulated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers these loans actually touch, the protections address practices — fee stacking, single-premium insurance, balloon payments, no ability-to-repay check — that have repeatedly ended in foreclosure, and the credit-tightening cost falls on a market segment that was often harming borrowers. The main honest objection is that some creditworthy-but-marginal borrowers could lose access to nonprime credit, but the bill's design (limits aimed at the most abusive loan terms rather than rate caps) blunts that risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Sarbanes introduced the bill on May 1, 2002, with 15 Democratic cosponsors including senior Banking Committee members.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders originating high-cost mortgages, mortgage brokers, and single-premium credit insurers kept the existing rules, since no competing predatory-lending measure advanced either in this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Paul Sarbanes
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland and chair of the Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and never brought it to a committee vote; the record shows no action after referral.

for.name: 15 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Dodd, Schumer, Kennedy, Durbin, Clinton, Boxer, and Levin.

against.name: Subprime mortgage lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal predatory-lending restrictions that would curtail prepayment penalties, financed credit insurance, and broker fee revenue; no Senate action followed the referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters were Democrats and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how the other 82 senators would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would cut off revenue from prepayment penalties, financed points and fees, balloon payments, and loan flipping, and would force an ability-to-repay check before lending against a home. Its death left those practices untouched.

The bill bans financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, and property insurance in high-cost mortgages — a product whose up-front premium added to the loan debt while often providing little value. The prohibition never took effect.
All broker compensation, direct or indirect, would count against the 3%/$600 financed-fee cap, squeezing broker yield on high-cost loans. The cap never became law in this Congress.

The bill would have required lenders to give borrowers a list of HUD-approved counseling agencies before closing a high-cost loan, steering borrowers toward counseling before signing. It never took effect.
